The meaning of the root ä is water in a very broad sense, referring to
liquid and juice in general:
ä-chïchïhualli  ´milk´; ä-xïxtli  ´urine´; ä-octli  ´vino hecho de miel y
agua´; ä-pätzcalli  ´water squeezed from plants´; ä-pïtzalli  ´diarrhea´;
ïx-äyötl  ´tears´; necu-ätl  ´unfermented maguey juice´; nex-ätl  ´lime
water´; xöch-ätl  ´rose water´.

We consider ca and a´ two variants of the same root. They are in compli-
mentary distribution. In 16th century Nahuatl in the Valley of Mexico ca
occurred after certain adverbs, mä ca, intlä ca, whereas a´ occurred
initially, e.g. a´-mö, a´-yäk, etc.

This particle occurs only with other particles, for example a´-zo and a´-
no-zo. Launey (1986, 8.1.2.2.5.3; pp. 1204-1207) suggests that a´ may be a
variant of at and discusses the use of a´-zo and a´-no-zo.
Cf. also our note to the root entry at.

Cf Launey 1986, 5.2.6.1.1, p. 648, "acâ a un premier /a/ bref (cet abrègement
se retrouve dans la formation des indéfinis locatifs). Il n´est pas impossible
que cette voyelle brève représente la forme de base, et que la voyelle longue
des interrogatifs doive être introduite par une règle spécifique."

A form of this root, ellel-, is found in two verbs, elleloa and elleltia,
and compounded in ellelaci, ellelaxitia, ellelcehuia, ellelmati,
ellelmachtia, ellequiza, ellelquixtia, elleltemi. We have evidence from
Carochi, fol. 112r, p. 516, and from Molina, fol. 35v, that ellelaci
´suffer/tener pena´ is constructed with the personal possessor prefixes
rather than with subject prefixes; whether this is also true for these
other intransitive verbs is so far uncertain. From the transitive ones
Molina gives nin. or nite. which can be either subject prefix + possessor
prefix or subject prefix + object prefix.

from the 16th century - and eventually till today - we register ilhuiä as
a root.

The sequence pil has a variety of different meanings; it appears compounded
with other roots, as an affix, and also independently.
So far we have distributed the occurrences on two roots and an affix. The two
roots are pil ´hang´ and pil ´child´. In identifying the word pilli ´child´
with the word pilli ´noble´ we simply follow the tradition.
However, when we identify pil in the word metlapilli ´mano de metate´ with
the root for ´child´, we base it on the observation that in other Mesoamerican
languages the word for ´mano de metate´ has the meaning ´child of the metate´,
this is true of various Mayan languages, some Mixe languages, Zapotec, and
probably others.
We have no similar argument for the words mapilli ´finger and xopilli ´toe´.
In the word cuitlapilli ´tail´ we consider the sequence pil an affix, but not
with much conviction; concerning the word nenepilli ´tongue´ we have put off
the decision; and in topilli (both vowels are long) the sequence is part of
the root topil.

We recognize three distinct roots:
1) tema ´heat in oven´;
2) tëmi, which underlies the word tëma, ´pour, put down (smthn. like corn)´;
3) tëmi ´swell, be filled´.
This decision is based on Carochi´s observation (f.128r, p.532) concerning
minimal pairs:
"Tëma nic, 1. larga, echar maiz, trigo, reales, &c. téma nic 1. breue, bañar
en temazcal, assar en hornillo, ò barbacoa".
It conflicts with Molina´s interpretation. He has two entries:
"Tema. nino. bañarse en temazcalli."
"Tema. nitla. echar o poner algo en alguna parte, assi como mayz. &c. o
cozer algo en hornillo pequeño." (f.96v).

This verbal root has a general meaning of loosening an object or making it
completely free from whatever it is fastened onto or contained in:
launch a ship; sing a song; peel off bark; scale a fish; take horns off an
animal; take bones out; for a bird to molt; dig up a corpse; take soot off
walls; remove the shoe from a horse; plant beans, probably take them out of
the pod; wag a tail; swing the arms; throw, i. e. make free from hand,
atlatl, gun, or whatever; etc.

The second vowel of this root is marked long in a few examples in Carochi´s
Arte, but in most of the examples it is unmarked. According to Karttunen
1983, it is specifically marked short in the Bancroft ms. In several modern
dialects, Coatepec Costales, La Huasteca, it is short, but in others it is
long, Tetelcingo, Xallitla.

This is not a true root. But we need a convincing analysis of the
word -tlAxIlA-kal+li in order to identify the actual root.

Carochi, (f.16v; p.415) writes "el tle tiene saltillo, si se le sigue
consonante, como tlè taxtica? que estas haciendo?" However, his examples
show unsystematic variation and do thus not confirm his suggestion. See
Launey (1986, 5.2.6.1.1; p. 646) for a discussion of the two variants,
tle/tle´.
See also the root -itl.
